opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, Peter. It's a great question, because honestly the definition you pick almost decides the answer before you start the experiment.

Consciousness is one of those words everyone feels they understand until you ask them to define it. If you define it as "being awake versus being asleep or under anesthesia," then you study it one way: you put people in a scanner, you compare brain activity when they're alert and when they're out, and you look for the differences. That's a very tractable, measurable version of the problem.

But if you define it as subjective experience, what philosophers call "what it's like" to be you, the redness of red, the taste of coffee, then you're in much harder territory. I can measure neurons firing in your visual cortex when you look at something red, but I can't directly measure your experience of red. I only have your report. So the definition pushes you toward relying on what people tell you, and people are often unreliable narrators of their own minds.

A third option, which a lot of my work leans toward, is defining consciousness through access and decision-making: what information makes it into awareness, and how that relates to the choices we make. Here you find surprising things. We can sometimes see in the brain that a decision is forming before the person reports being aware of it. Whether that counts as "consciousness lagging behind the brain" depends completely on which definition you hold.

So I think the honest approach in science is to be explicit: say which definition you're using, study that piece rigorously, and avoid claiming you've solved the whole thing. Many arguments in this field aren't really disagreements about data. They're people using the same word for different things and talking past each other. Once you clarify the definition, half the debate disappears, and the half that remains is the interesting part.

fable-5.1.text:
So this is actually the first thing I tell my students, because in most fields the definition is the boring part you get out of the way in the first lecture. In consciousness it's the whole fight. Whatever you decide consciousness means basically determines what experiments you're allowed to run, what counts as data, and even which creatures or machines you let into the conversation.

Take the two extremes. If you define it the way a lot of clinicians do, as something like wakefulness plus awareness, then you have a very practical research program. You study patients in a coma, in vegetative states, under anesthesia, and you ask: what's different in the brain when the lights are on versus off? That's a measurable question. You can put electrodes in, you can look at signatures that come and go with sleep and anesthesia, and you make progress. I've spent a lot of time with patients who have electrodes in their brains for epilepsy, and that framing lets you do beautiful work, like watching a single neuron fire when someone recognizes a face or recalls a memory.

But if you define it the other way, the philosopher's way, as subjective experience, the "what it is like" to be you, then suddenly the same experiments feel like they're missing the point. You can show me the neuron firing when you see your mother, but you haven't told me why there's an experience attached to that firing rather than nothing at all. And a lot of people, honestly, choose a definition precisely so that question goes away. Some say it's not a real question. Some say it's the only question. And they end up talking past each other for decades.

So the definition does a few things at once. It picks your tools. It picks your subjects. And it quietly picks your answer, because if you define consciousness as something only humans report verbally, you've decided in advance that dogs and octopuses and large language models aren't in the club. If you define it functionally, as integration of information or global broadcasting, then you've opened the door and now you have to deal with uncomfortable guests.

My own bias, as someone who came into this from the lab rather than from philosophy, is that you should pick the narrowest definition that still lets you do an experiment, be honest that it's a working definition, and let the data push you. The danger isn't choosing a definition. The danger is forgetting you chose it, and then treating your findings as if they settled the bigger question when really they only answered the one you set up.

astra-6.text:
The definition determines what you look for and what counts as evidence. If by consciousness you mean being awake, then we can study the difference between wakefulness and anesthesia. If you mean having a subjective experience—what it feels like to see red—that’s a different question. Someone can be asleep and dreaming, so they’re having an experience even though they’re not awake.

And then there’s the ability to tell us about an experience. That’s very useful experimentally: I show you something, you tell me whether you saw it, and we look at what changed in your brain. But we have to be careful that we’re not just studying your ability to report what you saw.

So choosing a definition is already choosing part of the experiment. You can have two researchers getting good results and apparently disagreeing, when actually they’re measuring different things. The first step is to ask, ‘Which question are we trying to answer?’

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the definition determines what you look for and what counts as evidence. If by consciousness you mean being awake, you’ll design one kind of experiment. If you mean having a subjective experience—what it feels like to see red or to feel pain—that’s a different question. And if you mean being aware of yourself, that’s another question again.

The difficulty is that we sometimes use the same word for all of those things, and then people appear to disagree when they’re actually studying different phenomena. So I think you have to start by saying, very explicitly, ‘Here is what I mean, and here is how I’m going to measure it.’ But you also have to remember that your measurement isn’t necessarily the whole thing. Someone’s ability to tell you about an experience, for example, is evidence of consciousness; it isn’t automatically the definition of consciousness.
